name: fastcpp::arena (developer source)
workload: Three microbenchmarks vs glibc new/delete on 200k 48-byte nodes: (A) bulk lifetime - allocate, fill, and free all nodes at once; (B) walk the list after allocation, measuring layout/locality only, no allocator calls; (C) churn - 200k allocate/free pairs in unrelated order with a bounded live set, a workload an arena structurally cannot serve.
claimed_speedup: 5.41x on bulk allocate+fill+free of 200k 48-byte nodes (3.451ns vs 18.682ns new/delete, results/fastest.json) / 5.4x in docs/allocators.md's own table (3.45ns vs 18.68ns); 4.75x on post-allocation list-walk locality (2.742ns vs 13.028ns for new fragmented by interleaved allocations). Cannot serve the churn workload (unrelated alloc/free order) at all; there the only lever is swapping the system allocator via LD_PRELOAD=jemalloc, which gives 2.71x over glibc new/delete and is not attributable to the arena.
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, 4 cores (SSE4.2, AVX2, BMI2, AVX-512F/VL, PCLMULQDQ); Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.18 (shared cloud VM)
tradeoffs: Individual objects can never be freed, only the whole arena at once (cursor reset), so it only suits objects that share one lifetime, e.g. one AST, one render frame, one parse. create<T> is static_assert'd to trivially-destructible types only because the arena never runs destructors. Cannot serve churn workloads (unrelated allocate/free order) at all. std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, in the standard library since C++17, gets within about 25% of the arena on the bulk-lifetime case (4.32ns vs 3.45ns).
caveats: Repo private:developer-source is PRIVATE and readable only via authenticated gh CLI, so despite full compiler/flags/CPU/commit disclosure this is capped below tier A per orchestrator instruction. Much of the locality win (suite B) is a glibc fragmentation artifact rather than an arena advantage: under LD_PRELOAD=jemalloc the same comparison shrinks from 4.75x to about 1.45x (3.965ns). Numbers are from a shared cloud VM; the results file's own caveat says absolute nanoseconds are not a reproducible spec, only within-row ratios are meaningful. docs/allocators.md separately argues, from the same data, that no allocator library should be vendored at all.

name: fastcpp::flat_hash_map (developer source)
workload: Per-lookup latency on 1M random uint64 keys (all-hit, all-miss, and build-from-empty), plus 200k string-key lookups using heterogeneous find(string_view), all against std::unordered_map.
claimed_speedup: 5.52x faster to build 1M uint64 keys from empty (34.72ns vs 191.71ns, one allocation for the table vs one node per entry); 2.18x faster on 200k string-key lookups (33.95ns vs 73.92ns); ~1.78x faster hit lookups and ~4.59x faster miss lookups on 1M uint64 keys (18.911ns vs 33.687ns; 9.723ns vs 44.665ns, derived from page data). Caveat from the same file/README: phmap::flat_hash_map (vendored in the same repo) beats fastcpp::flat_hash_map on raw lookup by 1.29x (hits) and 1.39x (misses), which is why fastcpp's own map is kept only for its faster from-empty build path.
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores; Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.18 (shared cloud VM)
tradeoffs: Open addressing invalidates pointers/references on growth, unlike node-based std::unordered_map; elements must be movable. Uses a wyhash-style hash_bytes rather than std::hash. phmap::flat_hash_map, vendored in the same repo, already beats this component's raw lookup speed by 1.29-1.39x, so this component's only remaining edge is the from-empty build path.
caveats: Repo private:developer-source is PRIVATE and readable only via authenticated gh CLI, so the benchmark code is not public; per orchestrator instruction this is capped below tier A despite full compiler/flags/CPU/commit disclosure. The results file's own caveat states absolute nanoseconds vary run to run on this shared cloud VM (elsewhere in the same file the same binary measured 3.42ns and 5.24ns for an identical lookup hours apart); only within-row ratios are meaningful.

name: fastcpp::io::buffered_writer (developer source)
workload: bench/bench_doing_less.cpp writes 20,000 short lines ('line N\n') to a real file descriptor (/dev/null) through fastcpp::io::buffered_writer (64 KiB buffer, 4 total write(2) calls) versus calling write(2) once per line (40,010 syscalls total).
claimed_speedup: 67.17x faster than one write(2) per line (2.93ns vs 196.803ns per line, results/fastest.json row 'buffered_output'); reduces the syscall count from 40,010 to 4, i.e. four orders of magnitude fewer kernel entries
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04 / Linux 6.18, shared cloud VM (bench/bench_syscall.cpp additionally reports this host as 'Not affected' by Meltdown and retbleed, i.e. no KPTI/retpoline tax)
tradeoffs: Requires an explicit flush() or destructor call to guarantee bytes reach the sink (no per-write durability); the buffer is a heap allocation (std::unique_ptr<char[]>, default 64 KiB) sized once at construction; a write larger than the remaining buffer bypasses buffering and goes straight to the sink. In the same bench file, buffered_writer also beats std::ostringstream heavily for in-memory formatting, but that comparison is not the row captured in results/fastest.json.
caveats: PRIVATE repo, readable only via the authenticated gh CLI (private:developer-source), not publicly browsable -- capped at tier C rather than A despite full compiler/flags/CPU/commit metadata being stated in results/fastest.json, per instruction not to claim tier A for private code. The header's own comment history (include/fastcpp/io/buffered_writer.hpp) originally claimed 'a write(2) costs 1-3us'; bench/bench_syscall.cpp later measured a real write(64B) to /dev/null at ~112ns and a bare kernel entry (getppid) at ~100ns on this unmitigated host -- roughly an order of magnitude below the original claim, because syscall entry cost is dominated by speculative-execution mitigations (KPTI/retpoline), which this host lacks. The repository's own text is explicit that this correction does not weaken the buffered_writer result: the count reduction (40,010 -> 4 syscalls) holds regardless of the per-syscall cost, but the previously advertised per-call nanosecond saving was overstated. Shared cloud VM: results/fastest.json's own caveat states absolute nanoseconds are not stable across runs or CPU-clock changes -- only ratios within one row are meaningful.

name: ConsensusRecSplit
workload: Construction of MPHFs over 100 million random string keys (length 10-50), comparing achieved bits/key against construction time versus RecSplit.
claimed_speedup: At 1.489 bits/key, ConsensusRecSplit constructs more than 350x faster than RecSplit, the previous state of the art at that space; given about an hour of construction time, it reaches 1.4448 bits/key (vs. a 1.4427 bit/key lower bound), where RecSplit only reaches 1.6127 bits/key in the same time.

name: emphf
workload: Construction of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, comparing emphf against CMPH's CHD algorithm (mphf_benchmark table) and, separately, against the 'phf' library in rchikhi/benchmphf's own 1-billion-key test.

Separately, rchikhi/benchmphf reports emphf's HEM variant building a 1-billion-key MPHF in 770s using 24GB RAM, versus the 'phf' library's 3900s and 48GB (about 5x faster, half the memory) -- that second comparison does not include CMPH numbers on the same page.

name: LeMonHash
baseline: Hollow Trie / Centroid Hollow Trie / ZFast Trie / PaCo Trie (prior state-of-the-art monotone minimal perfect hash function techniques); functionally these replace a sorted-array binary search or std::map rank query
workload: Rank queries (monotone minimal perfect hashing) over synthetic 64-bit integer datasets (uniform/normal/exponential, 100M keys) and real-world datasets (text, dna, urls, 5gram, fb, osm; 35M-800M keys), measuring query throughput, construction throughput, and bits/key vs prior MMPHF techniques
claimed_speedup: About 16x faster queries at 34% less space than the next larger competitor on synthetic integer data; up to 19x faster queries on real-world data at similar space; up to 2x faster construction than the next-best-space competitor (Hollow Trie variants); LeMonHash-VL (string variant) achieves up to 3x faster queries than the next larger competitor within 13% of its space
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.3GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.10.0, single-threaded
tradeoffs: GPLv3 is copyleft (no permissive reuse in proprietary code); like all MPHFs it returns arbitrary output for keys outside the original set; monotone MPHFs preserve key order (unlike plain MPHFs), which is a narrower guarantee that costs more space than a non-order-preserving MPHF; needs epsilon tuning for the PGM bucket mapper and depends on the BuRR retrieval structure and PGM-index as building blocks
caveats: Competitors benchmarked include Java implementations run on OpenJDK with JIT warm-up (author's own comparison notes Java is expected to be close to C++ performance, per prior work); comparison is against academic MMPHF implementations, not against std::map/std::unordered_map directly; each experiment run only twice and averaged (paper states variation is small)
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MPHF" --sort stars -> ByteHamster/LeMonHash; cross-checked against arXiv:2304.11012 (ESA 2023)

name: PHast / PHast+ (bsuccinct-rs "ph" crate)
workload: MPHF construction (1 and 12 threads) and lookup on 5*10^7 and 5*10^8 uniformly random 64-bit integer keys; measures bits/key, query ns/key, and construction ns/key
claimed_speedup: At 5*10^7 keys: PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) reaches 1.94 bit/key, 10 ns/key query, 606 ns/key single-thread construction (69 ns/key at 12 threads), vs PTHash (lambda=5.0, EF) at 2.11 bit/key, 54 ns/key query, 577 ns/key construction (231 ns/key at 12 threads); PHast+ cuts single-thread construction to 61-140 ns/key (an order of magnitude faster than PHast) for 10-15 ns/key query (derived from page data, Table 5.2 of arXiv:2504.17918)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0, both with third-level (-O3-equivalent) and CPU-native optimizations enabled
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5600G @ 3.9 GHz, 6 cores / 12 threads, 384KB/3MB/16MB L1/L2/L3 cache
tradeoffs: PHast/PHast+ trade small space overhead (~1.8-2.3 bits/key) for very simple, fast bucket-placement queries; PHast+ construction is 5-9x faster than PHast single-threaded and parallelizes near-linearly; PtrHash overtakes PHast on very large key sets once evaluation becomes memory-bandwidth bound. The same crate also ships FMPH/FMPHGO, fingerprinting-based MPHFs designed as a faster/smaller alternative to BBHash.
caveats: The Table 5.2/5.3 comparison is against other modern MPHFs (PTHash, PTHash-HEM, PHOBIC, PtrHash, SIMDRecSplit, SicHash, FMPH, FMPHGO), not directly against std::unordered_map, CMPH, or BBHash. The paper explicitly states it excluded BBHash from its own tests 'due to FMPH' already dominating it (citing Beling's 2023 ACM JEA paper, DOI 10.1145/3596453), so the FMPH-vs-BBHash numbers themselves were not independently re-verified on an accessible page this session.

name: PTHash
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over up to 1 billion pseudorandom 64-bit integer keys, 8-thread construction on one machine, reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper.
claimed_speedup: At similar space (~3 bits/key), PTHash looks up 3-4.6x faster than BBHash (37-55 ns/key for PTHash C-C/D-D variants vs 170 ns/key for BBHash gamma=1) on 1 billion 64-bit keys, though BBHash constructs faster (253s vs 689-1042s for PTHash) at that setting.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3, -march=native (per PTHash SIGIR'21 paper methodology; same author/repo/hardware used for the reproduction table)
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Offline/batch construction only (not incremental); needs a 64-bit-bucket-id compile flag beyond 2^32 buckets; several encoder/bucketer configs (lambda, alpha, dense vs partitioned) must be tuned for the desired space/time trade-off.
caveats: Numbers come from a companion benchmark repo maintained by the same authors reproducing their own paper's table, not an independent third party. CMPH itself was not benchmarked directly: the PTHash authors state CMPH's FCH implementation was 'orders of magnitude slower' than their own faithful FCH reimplementation, so the CMPH comparison in the source table is via that reimplementation, not the CMPH library itself.

name: RSHash

workload: Query time for 35 million existing real k-mers looked up in MQF filters loaded to 60%, 70%, 80% and 90% capacity, with MQF's per-key 'label' feature used as a minimal perfect hash function and compared against BBHash-style MPHFs
claimed_speedup: ~10-fold faster query time than BBHash (MPHFs), with MQF query time reported as invariable across load factors (paper Additional file 1, Figure S6; abstract states "the labels serve as a minimal perfect hash function but are ~10 fold faster than BBhash")
